title: Material electrical constants for Saans scenes
source: ITU-R P.2040 Table 3 ("Material properties"), Recommendation ITU-R P.2040: Effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz. 'drywall' is the table's 'plasterboard'.

formula.imaginary_permittivity: epsilon_r'' = sigma / (2 * pi * f_Hz * epsilon_0), epsilon_0 = 8.8541878128e-12 F/m; at f in GHz this is 17.9751036 * sigma / f_GHz
formula.reflection_normal: |Gamma| at normal incidence from air onto a half-space: Gamma = (1 - sqrt(eta)) / (1 + sqrt(eta)), eta = epsilon_r' - j*epsilon_r''

evaluated_at_note: 2.437 GHz is 802.11 channel 6, the carrier the whole repository already uses (SimOptions::default, wifisense/sources/synthetic.py). Values are stored to 9 significant digits so they can be re-derived from a, b, c, d and checked, which both test suites do.
caveats: PROVENANCE. The a, b, c, d coefficients were written down from ITU-R P.2040 Table 3 without the Recommendation open alongside. The derived columns are arithmetic and are checked by both test suites, so an error in a coefficient propagates silently into a correct-looking table. Before anyone quotes these outside this repository, check the six rows against a copy of the Recommendation; 'brick' is the row most worth checking first.

reflection_normal is a single flat air/material interface, not a slab. A real wall has two interfaces and internal reflections (ITU-R P.2040 section 5.2); for a thin sheet such as drywall the slab response differs substantially and is frequency- and thickness-dependent. Treat the stored number as an order-of-magnitude bridge to the simulator's scalar wall_reflection, not as the reflectivity of a finished wall.

These are the generic table values. Real concrete varies with moisture and reinforcement by more than the difference between two rows here; reinforcement (rebar) is a conductive grid the table does not model at all.
Nothing in this file has been checked against a measurement made with this hardware. It is a sourced default, not a calibration.

concrete.note: 0.395 is within 1.3% of the 0.4 the existing simulator already uses for wall_reflection (rust/crates/saans-sim/src/scenario.rs, Room::default). That agreement was not arranged; it is a useful check that the scalar in the simulator is a concrete-like wall.

brick.note: The exponent d = 0.16 is far flatter than the other rows (0.78-1.34) and it is the coefficient I am least sure I have recalled correctly. The narrower validity range, 1-10 GHz, is also particular to this row. 2.437 GHz is inside it, but check this row against a copy of the Recommendation before quoting it anywhere load-bearing.

drywall.note: ITU-R P.2040 calls this 'plasterboard'. The slab caveat bites hardest here: a 12.5 mm sheet is a thin layer at 12.3 cm wavelength and its real reflectivity swings with thickness.

glass.note: Plain glass. Low-emissivity (coated) glazing carries a metallic film and behaves nothing like this; the Recommendation treats it separately and this table has no row for it.

wood.note: Dry wood. Moisture raises both constants sharply and the table does not parameterise it.

metal.note: A conductor: reflects essentially everything, transmits essentially nothing. A steel almirah is an opaque screen in this band, not a lossy dielectric. Object material only; no wall in these scenes is metal.

fabric.note: ITU-R P.2040 Table 3 has no row for fabric, and I am not confident of a permittivity for upholstery from any source I can cite, so none is given rather than invented. A sofa carries this material as a LABEL for the viewer; any physics layer must refuse it until someone supplies a sourced value. Upholstered furniture is in any case mostly air, foam and a human-scale amount of water, and behaves more like a weak lossy scatterer than like a wall.
